text:
That 17% mentioned as "how much faster 2080 Super is, compared to the 5700XT" is really deceptive, because a simple average does not reflect the reality. The card was 19 to 38% faster in 8 titles, 3 to 13% faster in 3 titles and only 1 to 4% slower in 2 titles. And that's at 1440p. Playing at 1440p it's not even worth considering. This is a true 4K card, this comparison is utterly useless.

It depends on what you play. Also percentages aren't the WHOLE picture. Absolute numbers matter as well. If 5700XT gives 40FPS and 2080Super gives 60FPS, that's a 50% increase for 75% more money. You can say it's not optimal in terms of price/performance BUT in terms of actual gameplay experience... going from 40 to 60 FPS is a HUGE difference and that is SURELY worth the extra 25% money over the optimal linear price/perf. increase.

But at 4K it's 26% faster ON AVERAGE for 75% extra money and still this does not correctly reflect the value. For a Metro Exodus player, this card offers 47% extra performance at 4K. That is a significant boost in performance. Sure, 75% more money, but it means going from 38 FPS to 56 FPS (drop a notch of detail here or there, bang, you got 60 solid), which is a much much better experience on a nice big 4K TV with 60Hz refresh. I reckon that it's really worth 75% extra cash in this case.

It's all about perspective.

I agree that nvidia prices are too high. But AMD fanboyism does not help to paint a correct perspective. Comparing this card that really has the grunt for 4K with a 1440p card like 5700XT is pointless. Learn to use your damn brains and see the larger picture before fanboying like pigeons.

@eubikedude  No, just no... AMD is the lesser of two evils, but they are not your friend. They got caught price-fixing before, and have been exposed for several terrible practices. they have a history of not supporting their architecture and cards with drivers long term when they are not performance leaders. They are a business. They happen to be less predatory, but they're not saviors.

The AMD "team" gave us a 12 core part because they could not achieve boost clocks needed to beat the 9900k in gaming, and have stable memory. The engineering samples were said to hit much higher clocks. So they went wide, and decided to make their mid tier CPUs 8-core and dropped a 12-core part at the top of the stack. This was a very smart move, as the productivity value of the part more than makes up for the 5-10% gaming deficiency. Overall AMD parts are the best price to performance, the highest productivity, and very similar in gaming... But they carry the high cost that Intel does at the top of the stack. The increased core and chiplet requirement would have severely ate into their margins otherwise.

The 3800x is a fake part that has almost the same performance out of box as the 3700x. No tweaks required. The only reason this exists is to allow them to price the 12-core parts higher, and allows them to gain back margin loss. With the 9900k price drops and lower cost of the z390 boards, the 3900x is not in the same price tier anymore. 

AMD is providing the X570 chipset at a higher cost, and not allowing manufacturers to release PCI 4.0 on older boards. This caused x570 pricing to be higher then previous-gen upgrades, even though it is not justifiable with the lack of headroom for overclocking of the 3000 parts. 

AMD also locked down the 5700 and 5700 XT with frequency locks, and a blower cooler. they did not want people to be able to overclock and hit the real performance level of these cards, as they didn't want to end of life the Radeon 7 cards. Unfortunately people bypassed those limitations, and exposed the performance caps. 

Bottom line is that this whole launch has been filled with terrible hardware support, poor drivers, and many many inconsistencies with what we are being told vs reality. Tell me does this sound like your friend? No, it is just another company that is slightly more consumer friendly.
